concepts.name: Deriving values during render instead of syncing state in Effects
Angular OnPush checks: input references and events
Reviewing scaffolded EF Core migrations for data loss

choices.text: Compute `const total = items.reduce(...)` in render; drop the state and Effect
Keep the Effect, and add `total` to its dependency array so it never goes stale
Move the calculation into `useLayoutEffect` so users never see a wrong total
Wrap `setTotal` in `startTransition` so the extra render gets a low priority

questions.explanation: A value that can be calculated from existing state or props shouldn't be state. The Effect version renders once with a stale `total` and then renders again; computing it during render is faster, simpler and always consistent. If the calculation were measurably expensive, `useMemo` would cache it. Tweaking the Effect's dependencies, timing or priority keeps the redundant state and the extra render.

sources.title: You Might Not Need an Effect
sources.claim: Values that can be calculated from props or state should be calculated during rendering, not kept in state and updated in an Effect, which renders once with a stale value and then re-renders; use useMemo only for expensive calculations; event-specific logic belongs in event handlers, not Effects.

questions.prompt: An `OnPush` `CartSummaryComponent` has `@Input() cart: Cart`. On a click, the parent runs `this.cart.items.push(item)`, and the summary doesn't update. Why?

choices.text: `OnPush` components update only when the browser window regains focus
Angular compares inputs deeply, and `push` runs after that comparison
The input still holds the same reference, so Angular sees no new input
`@Input()` values are copied once at creation, so later changes are lost

questions.explanation: An `OnPush` component (the default since Angular v22) is checked when it receives a new input value, compared by reference, or when an event is handled in it or its children. Mutating the array keeps the same `cart` reference, so the child is skipped. Pass a new object instead (`this.cart = { ...this.cart, items: [...this.cart.items, item] }`) or hold the cart in a signal.

sources.title: Skipping component subtrees
sources.claim: An OnPush component subtree is checked only when its root receives new inputs from a template binding (compared with ==) or when Angular handles an event in the subtree's root or its children; mutating an input object while keeping its reference doesn't trigger change detection. OnPush is the default since Angular v22.

questions.prompt: A teammate replaces the `FirstName` and `LastName` properties with one `FullName` property, runs `dotnet ef migrations add`, and wants to ship the scaffolded migration unchanged. What would you check and change before it reaches a production database?

model_answer.summary: Review it: EF scaffolds this as dropping two columns and adding one, which loses every name; rewrite it to add the new column, copy the data with SQL, then drop the old columns, and decide honestly whether `Down` can be reversed.
key_points: Always review scaffolded migrations: EF can't tell a rename or replacement from a drop plus an add, and it warns when an operation may lose data
As scaffolded, the migration drops `FirstName` and `LastName` and adds an empty `FullName`, losing every customer's name
Rewrite it: add `FullName` as nullable, fill it with `migrationBuilder.Sql("UPDATE ...")` (branching on `ActiveProvider` if you support several databases), make it required, then drop the old columns

Implement `Down` only if the old values can be rebuilt; splitting names back isn't reliable, so fail explicitly and rely on a backup, and once a migration is applied to a shared database, fix it with a new migration rather than removing it

questions.explanation: Migrations are code that runs against production data with schema-changing rights, so they deserve the same review as any other code. The scaffolder only compares model snapshots; it doesn't know your intent, so data-preserving steps are yours to add.

sources.title: Managing Migrations - EF Core
sources.claim: Always review scaffolded migrations: renaming a property scaffolds DropColumn plus AddColumn, which loses the data, so replace it with RenameColumn; to replace columns, add the new one as nullable, populate it with Sql, make it required, then drop the old ones; implement Down only if reversible, and don't remove migrations already applied to shared or production databases.

questions.prompt: Review a React product page: one Effect watches `product.isInCart` to show an "Added to cart!" toast, and another resets `selection` to `null` whenever the `items` prop changes. What would you change, and why?

model_answer.summary: Both are Effects doing work that belongs elsewhere: show the toast from the buy handler, and derive or adjust the selection during render rather than resetting it after the fact.
key_points: Effects are for code that runs because the component was displayed; event-specific logic, like the toast after a purchase, belongs in the event handler (a shared `buyProduct` function called by each button)
The `isInCart` Effect fires again whenever the page shows an item already in the cart, such as after a refresh, so the toast reappears wrongly

Instead of resetting `selection` in an Effect, keep `selectedId` in state and compute `selection = items.find(...)` during render (or adjust state during render, or reset a whole subtree with a `key`)
Syncing state in Effects costs an extra render with stale values and makes data flow harder to follow

questions.explanation: "You Might Not Need an Effect" is a common interview topic because these Effects look harmless and cause subtle bugs: repeated notifications and a frame of stale UI. The test is why the code runs: because the user did something (event handler), because the component is on screen (Effect), or because it follows from current data (render).

sources.title: You Might Not Need an Effect
sources.claim: Values that can be calculated from props or state should be calculated during rendering, not kept in state and updated in an Effect, which renders once with a stale value and then re-renders; use useMemo only for expensive calculations; event-specific logic belongs in event handlers, not Effects.

questions.prompt: Which of these makes Angular check an `OnPush` component that has received no new input?

choices.text: A `setTimeout` callback inside it changes a plain, non-signal class field
A `(click)` handler bound in that component's own template runs
Its parent component is checked because of an unrelated event
A property deep inside one of its input objects is reassigned

questions.explanation: Angular checks an `OnPush` subtree when its root gets a new input from a template binding or when Angular handles an event, such as a `(click)` binding, in that component or its children. A parent being checked doesn't reach into an `OnPush` child whose inputs didn't change, a mutation inside an input object keeps the same reference, and a timer changing a plain field isn't one of the triggers.

sources.title: Skipping component subtrees
sources.claim: An OnPush component subtree is checked only when its root receives new inputs from a template binding (compared with ==) or when Angular handles an event in the subtree's root or its children; mutating an input object while keeping its reference doesn't trigger change detection. OnPush is the default since Angular v22.

questions.prompt: You rename the `Name` property of `Customer` to `FullName` and run `dotnet ef migrations add`. What does EF Core typically scaffold, and what should you do?

choices.text: `RenameColumn`, since the model snapshot records the property rename
Nothing, since the column name keeps following the old property name
`AlterColumn`, which copies data to the new column in one transaction
`DropColumn` and `AddColumn`; replace them with `RenameColumn`

questions.explanation: EF Core usually can't tell a rename from dropping one column and adding another, so it scaffolds `DropColumn("Name")` and `AddColumn("FullName")`. Applied as-is, every customer's name is lost. Replace the two operations with `migrationBuilder.RenameColumn(name: "Name", table: "Customers", newName: "FullName")`, and treat the scaffolder's data-loss warning as a signal to review the code.

sources.title: Managing Migrations - EF Core
sources.claim: Always review scaffolded migrations: renaming a property scaffolds DropColumn plus AddColumn, which loses the data, so replace it with RenameColumn; to replace columns, add the new one as nullable, populate it with Sql, make it required, then drop the old ones; implement Down only if reversible, and don't remove migrations already applied to shared or production databases.

questions.prompt: A teammate replaces the `FirstName` and `LastName` properties with one `FullName` property, runs `dotnet ef migrations add`, and wants to ship the scaffolded migration unchanged. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: As scaffolded, it drops both columns and adds an empty one, losing every name
Add `FullName` as nullable, fill it with `migrationBuilder.Sql`, then drop the old columns
If names can't be split back reliably, `Down` should fail and rely on a backup
EF detects that it is a replacement and copies the existing data across automatically
Once applied to a shared database, fix a mistake by removing the migration

questions.explanation: EF can't tell a replacement from a drop plus an add, so the scaffolded migration drops `FirstName` and `LastName` and adds an empty `FullName`; it warns about possible data loss, and the migration must be reviewed. Rewrite it to add `FullName` as nullable, fill it with `migrationBuilder.Sql("UPDATE ...")` (branching on `ActiveProvider`), make it required, then drop the old columns. Implement `Down` only if the old values can be rebuilt; otherwise fail explicitly and restore from a backup. A migration applied to a shared database is never removed: add a corrective one.

sources.title: Managing Migrations - EF Core
sources.claim: Always review scaffolded migrations, since EF can't tell a rename from a drop and add and warns about data loss; when replacing columns, add the destination as nullable, populate it with Sql (branching on ActiveProvider), make it required and drop the sources; implement Down only when the values can be rebuilt, otherwise fail and restore from backup; don't remove a migration applied to a shared database.

questions.prompt: A React product page has one Effect that shows an "Added to cart!" toast when `product.isInCart` is true, and another that resets `selection` to `null` whenever the `items` prop changes. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The toast belongs in the buy handler, not in an Effect watching `isInCart`
The `isInCart` Effect shows the toast again after a refresh if it's in the cart
Keep `selectedId` in state and compute `selection` from `items` during render
Setting state in an Effect costs nothing: React applies it in the same render
Effects are the right place for logic caused by a particular user interaction

questions.explanation: Logic caused by a particular interaction belongs in the event handler: a shared `buyProduct` function can add to the cart and show the toast. The `isInCart` Effect fires whenever the page shows an item already in the cart, so the toast reappears after a refresh. Rather than resetting `selection` in an Effect, store `selectedId` and compute the selected item from `items` during render. Updating state in an Effect isn't free: React renders again with the new state, after first rendering with stale values.

sources.title: You Might Not Need an Effect
sources.claim: Event-specific logic such as an added-to-cart notification belongs in the event handler, since an Effect on isInCart shows it again on refresh; instead of resetting selection in an Effect, store the selected ID and compute the item during render; updating state in an Effect causes an extra render pass.
